passage: In the school library after the mock round, Jahnavi and Ganga sat with the score sheet and their teacher watching quietly. "Look," said Ganga, pointing. "Three geography questions wrong." Jahnavi nodded. "Every time it's about rivers and states." They did not blame each other. They borrowed a big atlas from the shelf and a fold-out map. All week they spent twenty minutes a day quizzing each other on rivers, capitals and mountains, pointing at the map. In the next mock round, they missed only one geography question. Jahnavi high-fived Ganga, and even the teacher smiled.

passage: My brother Zubin and his quiz partner Bhavna did a practice round in our living room on Sunday, and I read the questions. They got most of the science and all of the sports. Then came four questions on geography, the longest river in Asia, the capital of Kenya, and they sat there silently. I saw Bhavna look at Zubin, and Zubin look at the ceiling. The next day Bhavna came over with an atlas from the school library, and they pinned my old world map above the dining table. For a week, every evening, I heard them quizzing each other: "Nairobi!" "Yangtze!" On the next Sunday I read a new set. They missed only one geography question.

qa.q: What did they pin above the dining table?
qa.a: They pinned an old world map above the dining table.

qa.q: What might Zubin have felt when he looked at the ceiling during the geography questions?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed and stuck, though the observer can only guess from the silence.

qa.q: What else could Zubin and Bhavna do now that geography is better?
qa.a: They could run another mock round across all topics to find the next weak area.

qa.q: How does the week look to the sibling reading the questions?
qa.a: The sibling sees the silence turn into shouted answers, and probably enjoys seeing the practice work.

grounding: It shows a quiz team finding in a mock round that they miss geography, spending a week with a map and atlas and improving their score.

Tuesday: Vishal and Sahil did a mock quiz with their teacher and scored 18 out of 30. Afterwards Sahil looked at the marked sheet. "Look. Every question we lost was geography." Vishal groaned. "I hate maps."
Friday: They had borrowed the big atlas from the library. Each evening they took one continent. Sahil read out a country, and Vishal found it and named the capital. Vishal still grumbled but pointed faster each time.
The next Tuesday: A new mock quiz. This time they scored 25. They got four of the five geography questions right. Vishal grinned at the map on the classroom wall like it was an old enemy he had beaten.

How did Vishal feel when he heard all the lost questions were geography?
qa.a: He felt fed up and reluctant, groaning that he hated maps.

qa.q: How does the new score look to Sahil?
qa.a: Sahil sees that spotting the weak topic and working on it paid off, so Sahil probably feels proud.

grounding: It shows a quiz team spotting geography as a weak topic after a mock round, practising with an atlas and improving their score.
